content: Lower limb muscle cramps are a common and painful condition that can significantly impair an individual’s ability to participate in physical activities, disrupt sleep, and reduce overall quality of life. Various interventions have been proposed to address this issue, but some are controversial, potentially harmful, or ineffective. This review focuses on non-drug, non-invasive therapies for the secondary prevention of lower limb muscle cramps, updating a previous Cochrane Review from 2012 to include new evidence. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of non-drug, non-invasive interventions on lower limb muscle cramps. The primary outcome assessed was the frequency of cramps, while secondary outcomes included cramp pain severity, cramp duration, health-related quality of life, sleep quality, daily activity participation, the proportion of participants experiencing cramps, and adverse events. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that tested non-drug, non-invasive interventions for at least four weeks in individuals with lower limb muscle cramps, excluding pregnant women. Searches were conducted in August 2018 and May 2020 across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Neuromuscular Specialised Register, without restrictions on language or publication date. Three trials involving 201 participants aged 50 years and older were included in the review. None of the participants had neurological diseases. All three trials investigated the effects of stretching exercises on lower limb muscle cramps. 1. Combination of Calf and Hamstring Stretching for Six Weeks: In individuals aged 55 years and older, a combination of daily calf and hamstring stretching for six weeks may reduce the severity of night-time lower limb muscle cramps. This was measured using a 10 cm visual analogue scale (VAS), where 0 represents no pain and 10 represents the worst pain imaginable. The mean difference (MD) in cramp severity was -1.30 (95% confidence interval [CI] -1.74 to -0.86) compared to no intervention. However, the certainty of this evidence was low. The evidence for the effect of this intervention on cramp frequency was very uncertain. The change in the number of cramps per night from week zero to week six showed a mean difference of -1.2 (95% CI -1.8 to -0.6), but the certainty of this evidence was very low. 2. Calf Stretching Alone for 12 Weeks: In individuals aged 60 years and older, calf stretching alone for 12 weeks may have little to no effect on the frequency of night-time lower limb muscle cramps. The median number of cramps in the last four weeks was 4 (interquartile range [IQR] 8) in the stretching group and 3 (IQR 7.63) in the sham stretching group. Statistical analysis (U = 973.5, z = -0.995, P = 0.32, r = 0.10) indicated no significant difference. The certainty of this evidence was low. This trial did not report on cramp severity. 3. Combination of Calf, Quadriceps, and Hamstring Stretching in Women with Metabolic Syndrome: In women aged 50 to 60 years with metabolic syndrome, the evidence is very uncertain regarding the effects of a combination of daily calf, quadriceps, and hamstring stretching on the frequency and severity of leg cramps. The frequency data could not be fully analyzed, and the scale used to measure cramp severity was not validated. None of the included studies reported on health-related quality of life, sleep quality, or participation in daily activities. Additionally, no adverse events were reported by participants in any of the three studies. However, the evidence for adverse events was of moderate certainty, as the small sample sizes of the studies may not have been sufficient to detect uncommon events. The review identified several limitations in the included studies. Two of the three studies were at risk of recall bias, and the tools used to measure outcomes were not validated. Furthermore, the small sample sizes and imprecise findings with wide confidence intervals limit the reliability of the results. These methodological issues make it uncertain whether future studies will yield similar findings. In conclusion, daily calf and hamstring stretching for six weeks may reduce the severity of night-time lower limb muscle cramps in individuals aged 55 years and older, but its effect on cramp frequency remains uncertain. Calf stretching alone for 12 weeks may have little to no effect on cramp frequency in individuals aged 60 years and older. The evidence regarding the effects of combined stretching exercises in women with metabolic syndrome is very uncertain. The lack of validated outcome measures and inconsistent diagnostic criteria across studies makes it challenging to compare findings and apply them to clinical practice. Given the prevalence and impact of lower limb muscle cramps, there is an urgent need for well-designed RCTs to evaluate commonly recommended and emerging non-drug therapies. Future research should also focus on developing and validating specific tools to measure cramp-related outcomes.
